title: Bay FC close to appointing ex-Chelsea general manager Paul Green as head of football
content:
Bay FC is in the final stages of adding Paul Green as its head of football, according to sources with knowledge of the ongoing negotiations.

Green was a key piece of Chelsea Women’s front office for 13 years alongside former head coach Emma Hayes, the current USWNT coach.

It represents a major addition to Bay FC’s front office as the club addresses their performance issues over the past two seasons, after making the playoffs in their inaugural season in 2024.

Chelsea parted ways with Green in February after his longstanding tenure with the club as its general manager. He was widely regarded to be one of the main — if largely unseen — architects of the club’s success in the Women’s Super League, helping the club win 19 major trophies.

Green first joined Chelsea in February 2013 as part of Hayes’ coaching staff, initially as her assistant, and he was later appointed the club’s general manager. He was tasked with player recruitment, helping to build one of English women’s football’s most impressive squads, and was central figure in appointing Sonia Bompastor as Hayes’ successor in 2024.

His role with Bay FC would be entirely dedicated to the NWSL club, not the ownership group’s larger project, Bay Collective. Sources indicated that once his hiring is official, he will report to Kay Cossington, the CEO of Bay Collective.

Bay FC is currently 15th in the NWSL standings, winning six games through their 22 played so far this season.

Bay FC declined to comment when contacted by The Athletic.

Analysis from women’s soccer writer Tamerra Griffin

The Bay Area has historically been home to some of the most successful youth soccer clubs, college teams, and professional women’s programs in the country. The founding owners of Bay FC all have deep ties to the region — yet increasingly, the front office of the San Jose-based club looks more and more like an English institution.

Green is the latest marker of this transformation, which was preceded by the hiring of Emma Coates and her assistant Gemma Davies last December, who both previously worked with England’s Under-23 and Under-19 sides, and the appointment of Cossington, the English Football Association’s former technical director, as the CEO of the multi-club ownership platform Bay Collective, of which Bay FC is a part.

At the same time, even if Bay FC weren’t trending in that direction, they would have always been remiss not to pursue Green. His resume with Chelsea speaks for itself, and considering the struggles Bay FC has had with its roster construction, he will inevitably play a huge role in recruiting players, establishing standards, and spearheading short- and long-term planning.

There’s also Green’s network to consider, an asset that in itself holds significant value. His relationships with clubs and national teams all over the world align with the international approach Bay FC has demonstrated since its inaugural season. His presence could do wonders to soothe concerns about the club’s current standing from a recruitment standpoint, and is an important show of Bay FC’s commitment to gather the pieces to build a club capable of righting itself after two poor seasons.
